Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: Prioritisation: why ABC beats everything else
Hook: When two patients both need you, the order is not a judgement call.
Australian practice: Australian emergency departments triage on the Australasian Triage Scale (ATS 1-5).
Common trap: Choosing the most thorough action when the question asked for the first action.
Resource: ACSQHC: Recognising and responding to acute deterioration

Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: Delegation: what you can and cannot hand over
Hook: You can delegate the task. You can never delegate the accountability.
Australian practice: Australia's skill mix is RN, Enrolled Nurse and Assistant in Nursing. An EN works under the direction of an RN and is implementation-focused, so an EN does not independently assess or plan care.
Common trap: Assuming an Enrolled Nurse can do an initial assessment because they are registered.
Resource: NMBA: Enrolled Nurse Standards for Practice

Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: Scope of practice: the question to ask before you act
Hook: Scope is set by your education and competence, not by your job title.
Australian practice: Australia uses the NMBA's national Decision-Making Framework, a set of structured questions you work through before performing an activity, covering education, competence, authorisation and evidence.
Common trap: Treating a local ward habit as authorisation.

Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: ISBAR: the handover structure that is mandated here
Hook: Most handover failures are missing the last letter.
Australian practice: ISBAR is mandated nationally under NSQHS Standard 6 (Communicating for Safety) and is an accreditation requirement in Australian hospitals, so it is the expected structure for every escalation call.
Common trap: Leaving out the Recommendation and hoping the other person infers what you need.

Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: Informed consent: whose job is it
Hook: The nurse witnesses consent. The nurse does not obtain it.
Australian practice: There is no single national consent law in Australia. Each state and territory has its own guardianship and consent legislation, so capacity and substitute consent processes vary by jurisdiction.
Common trap: Proceeding because the form is signed, when the patient no longer understands what is planned.
Resource: End of Life Law in Australia: Capacity and consent

Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: Advance care directives and who decides
Hook: The family disagrees with the directive. What happens?
Australian practice: Terminology is state-based: 'Person Responsible' in NSW, 'Medical Treatment Decision Maker' in Victoria, 'Enduring Guardian' elsewhere. There is no single national living-will equivalent.
Common trap: Following the loudest family member instead of the correctly ranked decision-maker.
Resource: End of Life Law in Australia: State and territory laws

Week theme: Thinking like a nurse, prioritisation and professional practice
Topic: Advocacy: representing their wishes, not your opinion
Hook: Advocacy means their choice, even when you would choose differently.
Australian practice: Cultural safety is an explicit obligation in the NMBA Code of Conduct, including a specific requirement to provide culturally safe care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
Common trap: Overriding an informed refusal because you believe you are advocating for their health.
Resource: NMBA: Code of Conduct for Nurses
Sunday story (this week): Introduce the 10-week syllabus and ask people to comment 'in' if they are starting with you. No link.

Topic: Confidentiality: need-to-know, every time
Hook: No names in the lift. No details in the tearoom.
Australian practice: Australia is governed by the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles, plus state health records legislation. My Health Record has its own access and consent rules.
Common trap: Assuming family have a right to information because they are next of kin.

Topic: Who to refer to, and when
Hook: Coordinating care is a skill the exam tests directly.
Australian practice: Community allied health is often accessed through a GP Chronic Disease Management Plan, which attracts Medicare rebates for a set number of sessions.
Common trap: Managing it yourself when a scope-appropriate referral is clearly indicated.

Topic: Discharge planning starts on admission
Hook: If discharge planning starts on discharge day, it has already failed.
Australian practice: Aged care and disability supports are arranged through My Aged Care and the NDIS, with ACAT assessment determining aged-care eligibility.
Common trap: Recording education as complete because a pamphlet was handed over.

Topic: Ethical conflict and conscientious objection
Hook: You object to the procedure. Can you step away?
Australian practice: Ethical obligations are codified nationally in the NMBA Code of Conduct, which applies in every state and territory.
Common trap: Withdrawing care without ensuring someone else has taken it over.
Resource: NMBA: Code of Conduct for Nurses

Topic: Mandatory notification: an obligation unique to here
Hook: In Australia, reporting an impaired colleague can be a legal duty.
Australian practice: AHPRA mandatory notification is a defined legal obligation on every registered practitioner in Australia, made directly to the regulator.
Common trap: Treating an impaired colleague as an internal HR matter only.

Topic: Open disclosure: saying sorry is not admitting liability
Hook: Something went wrong. The patient is told, promptly, and honestly.
Australian practice: Open disclosure is a formal national requirement under the NSQHS Standards and the Australian Open Disclosure Framework. Under most state Civil Liability Acts an apology is not an admission of liability.
Common trap: Staying silent about a near-miss because the patient was not harmed.

Topic: The 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene
Hook: Five moments. Most missed is the one after touching the surroundings.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Delivered nationally through Hand Hygiene Australia with mandatory audit and compliance reporting feeding into NSQHS Standard 3 accreditation.
Common trap: Using alcohol rub after caring for a patient with C. difficile. Spores need soap and water.
Sunday story (this week): Recap the week's four legal and professional posts in one frame. Ask what topic they want covered next. No link.

Topic: Contact, droplet or airborne: matching the precaution
Hook: Match the organism to the precaution. This is a guaranteed exam pattern.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Australia says P2/N95 respirator, and follows the NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare.
Common trap: A surgical mask for suspected tuberculosis or measles. It must be a fit-tested respirator.
Resource: NHMRC, Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare

Topic: ANTT: the term used here instead of 'sterile technique'
Hook: Key parts and key sites. Protect those and you have protected the patient.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Aseptic Non-Touch Technique is the nationally endorsed framework in Australia and is embedded in NSQHS Standard 3 competency assessment, and it is the language used on Australian competency documents.
Common trap: Treating every aseptic procedure as needing full surgical technique.
Resource: ACSQHC: Preventing and Controlling Infections Standard

Topic: Multi-resistant organisms and stewardship
Hook: Resistance is a system problem, not just a prescribing one.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: National surveillance runs through ACSQHC's AURA system, and stewardship is mandated under NSQHS Standard 3 rather than left to individual hospital programmes.
Common trap: Standing precautions down because the infection was treated.

Topic: Sharps injury: the first five minutes
Hook: Wash it. Report it now. Do not squeeze it.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Managed under state health department policy and notified through the state SafeWork regulator. Hepatitis B vaccination and titre checks are a standard Australian pre-employment requirement.
Common trap: Waiting until the shift ends to report, and losing the prophylaxis window.
Resource: NSW Health: Occupational exposure to blood-borne viruses

Topic: Manual handling: use the hoist
Hook: The correct answer is almost never 'get another nurse to lift'.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Governed by Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on Hazardous Manual Tasks under state WHS Acts, which sets out the assess-and-control duty in detail.
Common trap: Choosing a two-person manual lift when a hoist is available and indicated.
Resource: Safe Work Australia: Hazardous Manual Tasks Code of Practice

Topic: Restrictive practices: last resort, always reviewed
Hook: A lap belt can be a restrictive practice. Intent and effect decide.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Australia regulates these formally as 'restrictive practices', through the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission for disability, and state Mental Health Acts for mental health. Reduction targets sit in NSQHS Standard 5, as a rights-based national scheme.
Common trap: Assuming bed rails are automatically not a restraint.

Topic: RACE: the fire response order
Hook: Rescue. Alert. Contain. Extinguish, and only if it is safe.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Australian hospitals use EWIS emergency warning systems with coded alerts under AS 3745, and the Australasian Triage Scale for mass casualty prioritisation.
Common trap: Trying to extinguish a spreading fire instead of evacuating.
Sunday story (this week): Poll: which of this week's infection-control facts did you not know? Still no link.

Topic: Two identifiers, every single time
Hook: Two identifiers. Never the bed number.
NCLEX category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
Australian practice: Falls and pressure injury screening are mandated under NSQHS Standard 5, and a deteriorating patient is escalated with a MET call, any staff member can activate it directly, without waiting for a doctor.
Common trap: Waiting for the treating team before escalating a patient who already meets MET criteria.

Topic: APINCHS: the high-risk medicines acronym used here
Hook: Seven letters that cover most serious medication harm.
Australian practice: APINCHS is the ACSQHC national framework for high-risk medicines, and Australian workplaces name it directly on charts, storage rules and double-check policies.
Common trap: Believing a double-check alone prevents error. Storage and system design matter just as much.

Topic: Insulin: onset, peak, duration and the 15/15 rule
Hook: Rapid-acting peaks in 1 to 2 hours. Know when the risk lands.
Australian practice: Blood glucose is measured in mmol/L. A BGL of 3.2 mmol/L is hypoglycaemia and needs treating. Australian brand names include NovoRapid, Actrapid and Lantus.
Common trap: Seeing a single-digit BGL and not recognising it as hypoglycaemia.

Topic: Warfarin versus heparin: monitoring and reversal
Hook: Different test. Different antidote. Do not mix them up.
Australian practice: Vitamin K is called phytomenadione here (Konakion). Warfarin management guidance follows Australian Prescriber and local anticoagulation protocols.
Common trap: Giving vitamin K for a high INR with no bleeding, without checking the local threshold.

Topic: Opioids: sedation score before respiratory rate
Hook: Sedation comes before respiratory depression. That is your early warning.
Australian practice: Intranasal naloxone (Nyxoid) is TGA-approved and available through take-home naloxone programmes in Australian pharmacies. Brand names differ. Endone is oxycodone, Kapanol is modified-release morphine.
Common trap: Withholding all analgesia for mild sedation instead of adjusting the dose and continuing to monitor.
Resource: Australian Prescriber: Naloxone in the community

Topic: Vancomycin and gentamicin: the monitoring drugs
Hook: Red and flushed during a vancomycin infusion is usually a rate problem.
Australian practice: Antibiotic choice and dosing follow Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG), the national antimicrobial stewardship reference.
Common trap: Labelling infusion-rate flushing as anaphylaxis and withholding the drug permanently.

Topic: IV potassium is never a push
Hook: Undiluted IV potassium causes cardiac arrest. There is no exception.
Australian practice: Potassium is reported and prescribed in mmol/L, and NSW CEC publishes a specific high-risk potassium protocol setting concentration and rate limits.
Common trap: Choosing rapid correction by push for severe hypokalaemia. Always wrong.
Sunday story (this week): Share the medication-safety carousel again as a story. Mention that the syllabus is halfway to the halfway point. No link.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Digoxin, beta blockers and ACE inhibitors: check before you give
Hook: Count the apical pulse for a full minute. Then decide.
Australian practice: Australian brand confusion between digoxin products at different strengths has prompted specific safety advisories, always check the strength on the chart.
Common trap: Treating an ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema as the same level of concern.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Extravasation: leave the cannula in
Hook: Stop the infusion. Do not pull the cannula out yet.
Australian practice: IV fluids sit in the APINCHS 'Systems' category in Australia, so they carry the same high-risk handling requirements as other APINCHS medicines.
Common trap: Removing the cannula immediately and re-siting further down the same limb.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Blood transfusion: the first 15 minutes
Hook: Stay with them for the first 15 minutes. That is when reactions declare.
Australian practice: Governed by ANZSBT guidelines and Lifeblood processes, with Australian traceability documentation required for every unit.
Common trap: Watching a little longer before stopping when early reaction signs appear.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Medication calculation without the 1000-fold error
Hook: Convert the units first. Every time.
Australian practice: Weight is always in kilograms and volumes are metric. The National Inpatient Medication Chart standardises how doses are written and checked.
Common trap: Forgetting a microgram to milligram conversion mid-calculation, a 1000-fold error.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Anaphylaxis: adrenaline first, into the thigh
Hook: Adrenaline. Intramuscular. Anterolateral thigh. Nothing before it.
Australian practice: The drug is called adrenaline, and management follows ANZCOR Guideline 9.2.7.
Common trap: Giving an antihistamine first while assessing severity.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Track and trigger: escalation is not optional
Hook: Two yellows or one red. The chart tells you what to do.
Australian practice: Australia uses colour-zoned observation charts under Between the Flags, and deterioration is escalated by MET call.
Common trap: Being reassured by one abnormal observation because the others look fine.

Week theme: High-risk medicines and the first numbers
Topic: Australian lab reference ranges in SI units
Hook: Haemoglobin is reported in g/L. For a man, 130 to 170 g/L is the normal range.
Australian practice: Australian pathology reports in SI units, mmol/L, micromol/L and g/L, and the reference intervals are locally harmonised. Always check your own laboratory's stated range as well.
Common trap: Treating a haemoglobin of 140 g/L as abnormal when it sits mid-range.
Sunday story (this week): First mention of the readiness test. Frame it as 'find out which of these areas is actually below your level'. Link sticker.

Topic: ABG interpretation with ROME
Hook: Respiratory Opposite. Metabolic Equal. That is the whole method.
Australian practice: Australian laboratories may report gases in kPa as well as mmHg depending on the analyser. Check the unit before interpreting, 1 kPa is about 7.5 mmHg.
Common trap: Reading a kPa value as mmHg and reversing the interpretation.
Resource: Australian Prescriber: Interpreting arterial blood gases

Topic: Fasting before surgery: 6 and 2
Hook: Six hours for food. Two hours for clear fluids. Not midnight.
Australian practice: Fasting and pre-anaesthetic standards follow ANZCA, and GLP-1 agonist users have specific Australian periprocedural advice because of delayed gastric emptying.
Common trap: Applying an outdated nil-by-mouth-from-midnight rule.
Resource: ANZCA: Pre-anaesthesia consultation and patient preparation

Topic: Contrast, metformin and the shellfish myth
Hook: Which allergy actually matters before a contrast CT?
Australian practice: Contrast safety follows the RANZCR iodinated contrast guideline, which sets the eGFR thresholds and metformin hold times used here.
Common trap: Cancelling contrast because the patient mentioned a shellfish allergy.

Topic: Never clamp a bubbling chest drain
Hook: Clamping a bubbling drain can cause a tension pneumothorax.
Australian practice: None material, the principles are universal, though each health service has its own nursing procedure.
Common trap: Clamping the drain to move the patient.
Resource: Royal Children's Hospital: Chest drain management

Topic: Complications to anticipate after common procedures
Hook: Post-procedure back pain and low blood pressure is not 'normal recovery'.
Australian practice: None material for recognition; documentation goes through Australian incident and clinical governance systems.
Common trap: Attributing post-procedure hypotension to opioids without excluding bleeding.

Topic: Catheters: review the need every day
Hook: The best way to prevent a catheter infection is to remove the catheter.
Australian practice: Insertion follows Aseptic Non-Touch Technique, the standard Australian framework and terminology.
Common trap: Re-catheterising without scanning first.

Topic: Acute coronary syndrome: the first ten minutes
Hook: A 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes. That is the standard.
Australian practice: Diagnostic pathways follow Heart Foundation and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand high-sensitivity troponin protocols, resuscitation follows ANZCOR, and the emergency number is 000.
Common trap: Giving oxygen to every chest pain patient regardless of saturation.
Sunday story (this week): Story the cardiac reference card, then the readiness test link under it.

Topic: Heart failure: the daily weight is the early warning
Hook: Two kilograms in two days is fluid, not food.
Australian practice: The medication is spelled frusemide on Australian charts, not furosemide. Guidance comes from the Heart Foundation and CSANZ.
Common trap: Giving a fluid bolus to a breathless heart failure patient.

Topic: Stroke: the clock starts at last known well
Hook: Nil by mouth until someone has done the swallow screen.
Australian practice: Australia follows the Stroke Foundation's Living Clinical Guidelines, which are continuously updated as new evidence lands.
Common trap: Assuming every stroke gets thrombolysis. A bleed must be excluded on CT first.

Topic: Oxygen targets: when 88 to 92 percent is the goal
Hook: More oxygen is not always better. Sometimes it is the harm.
Australian practice: Australian practice prescribes oxygen against a documented target range following Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance, which is more explicit than ad-hoc high-flow practice elsewhere.
Common trap: Turning oxygen up because a COPD patient sits at 90%.

Topic: A silent chest in asthma is an emergency
Hook: No wheeze does not mean better. Sometimes it means barely moving air.
Australian practice: Severity grading and escalation follow the Australian Asthma Handbook from the National Asthma Council, and spacer-first practice is emphasised more strongly here.
Common trap: Documenting improvement because the wheeze has stopped.

Topic: Acute kidney injury and the sick day rules
Hook: Some medicines should be paused when someone is unwell and dehydrated.
Australian practice: eGFR is automatically reported on Australian pathology results, and Kidney Health Australia publishes 'sick day rules' telling patients which medicines to pause during illness, a distinctly Australian resource.
Common trap: Continuing metformin and NSAIDs through dehydration or contrast imaging.
Resource: Kidney Health Australia: CKD Management Handbook

Topic: DKA versus HHS: the numbers that separate them
Hook: Fluids first. Check the potassium. Then insulin.
Australian practice: Glucose and ketones are in mmol/L here. Euglycaemic DKA can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors, so a near-normal glucose does not exclude it.
Common trap: Starting insulin before fluids and before confirming potassium.

Topic: Compensated shock: normal blood pressure, abnormal patient
Hook: By the time blood pressure falls, compensation has already failed.
Australian practice: Deterioration triggers a MET call, with activation criteria set by the ACSQHC Recognising and Responding to Acute Deterioration Standard.
Common trap: Waiting for hypotension before escalating.
Sunday story (this week): Ask a question about the week's emergencies, then link the readiness test in the reply frame.

Topic: Sepsis: cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within the hour
Hook: Every hour of delay costs. The order still matters.
Australian practice: Australia runs the SEPSIS KILLS pathway and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard as the mandated national framework.
Common trap: Giving antibiotics before cultures and losing the diagnosis.

Topic: Hyperkalaemia: calcium protects the heart first
Hook: Calcium does not lower the potassium. It protects the heart while you do.
Australian practice: Electrolytes are reported and prescribed in mmol/L throughout Australia.
Common trap: Giving calcium and assuming the potassium is now treated.

Topic: Pain in dementia: use a behavioural tool
Hook: If they cannot tell you, you still have to measure it.
Australian practice: The Abbey Pain Scale was developed in Australia for residential aged care and is the most widely used Australian tool for dementia-related pain.
Common trap: Withholding analgesia because the observations look too normal for the reported pain.

Topic: Confirming a nasogastric tube: pH, not a whoosh
Hook: The whoosh test is not a test. Check the pH.
Australian practice: The Malnutrition Screening Tool was developed and validated in Queensland and is used as the standard across most Australian hospitals under the Comprehensive Care Standard.
Common trap: Relying on auscultation to confirm placement before feeding.

Topic: Bristol stool chart and bowel care that prevents harm
Hook: Constipation on opioids is predictable. So prevent it.
Australian practice: None material, the chart and principles are used internationally.
Common trap: Charting bowels not open for several days without acting on it.

Topic: Pressure injury staging in four steps
Hook: Stage 1 is intact skin that does not blanch. That is the one people miss.
Australian practice: Falls and pressure injury screening within a set time of admission are mandated under NSQHS Standard 5, and stage 3 or higher injuries are generally reportable clinical incidents.
Common trap: Recording non-blanchable redness as a bruise.

Topic: Sleep: cluster the care before reaching for sedation
Hook: The first intervention for poor sleep is not a tablet.
Australian practice: The Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety specifically flagged sedation overuse in Australian residential aged care, driving a strong national push to minimise pharmacological sleep aids.
Common trap: Giving a PRN sedative before trying environmental measures.
Sunday story (this week): Readiness test link, with the line about the report naming specific areas rather than giving a score.

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: Recognising the dying phase
Hook: At some point, routine observations stop being care.
Australian practice: Advance care directives are state-legislated with different names in each jurisdiction, and hyoscine butylbromide is commonly used in Australia for end-of-life secretions.
Common trap: Continuing 4-hourly observations on someone who is actively dying.

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: Supporting independence, not doing it for them
Hook: Doing it faster yourself is not always doing it better.
Australian practice: Equipment and home modifications are funded through the NDIS and My Aged Care, with occupational therapy home assessment standard before discharge. The term is walking frame, not walker.
Common trap: Completing the task for the person and undermining their rehabilitation.

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: Developmental red flags worth memorising
Hook: Not the milestones themselves, the ages they should have passed.
Australian practice: Australia uses the child health record ('blue book') and Key Ages and Stages checks through child and family health nurse services in every state and territory.
Common trap: Quoting a checkpoint age from memory instead of the Key Ages and Stages schedule.
Resource: Royal Children's Hospital: Kids Health Info

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: Antenatal danger signs that need review today
Hook: Headache, visual change and epigastric pain belong together.
Australian practice: Care follows the national Pregnancy Care Guidelines and RANZCOG, usually through midwifery continuity of care or GP shared care, with a visit schedule risk-stratified rather than fixed.
Common trap: Applying a fixed visit count instead of the risk-stratified Australian schedule.

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: APGAR, and the jaundice that is never normal
Hook: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological.
Australian practice: Newborn bloodspot screening occurs at 48-72 hours and hearing screening is universal. Vitamin K and the hepatitis B birth dose require documented parental consent, they are recommended, not automatic.
Common trap: Treating day-one jaundice as physiological.

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: Immunisation: the National Immunisation Program schedule
Hook: The National Immunisation Program sets the schedule, and it is reviewed regularly.
Australian practice: Australia follows the National Immunisation Program schedule and the Australian Immunisation Handbook. Adolescent doses are delivered through school programmes, and shingles vaccination is funded from 65, or from 50 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Common trap: Quoting a schedule from memory instead of checking the current handbook.

Week theme: End of life, and the start of life
Topic: Australian cancer screening: the three programmes
Hook: Cervical screening here starts at 25 and runs every 5 years.
Australian practice: Australia moved to five-yearly HPV-based cervical screening in 2017, and lowered bowel screening to start at age 45 from July 2024.
Common trap: Quoting an interval from memory instead of the current programme ages.
Sunday story (this week): Two frames: the end-of-life post that got the most saves, then the readiness test link.

Topic: Standard drinks and the NHMRC alcohol guidance
Hook: An Australian standard drink is 10 grams of alcohol.
Australian practice: An Australian standard drink contains 10 g of alcohol, and every NHMRC limit is counted against that measure. Pub and restaurant servings are often more than one standard drink.
Common trap: Counting glasses rather than standard drinks.

Topic: Therapeutic versus non-therapeutic responses
Hook: False reassurance feels kind. It closes the conversation.
Australian practice: None material, the technique is universal. Use Australian idiom in patient-facing phrasing.
Common trap: Choosing 'I'm sure it will be fine' over an open, validating response.

Topic: The mental state examination, domain by domain
Hook: Describe what you observed. Do not record your conclusion.
Australian practice: Mental health legislation is state and territory based in Australia, so involuntary assessment criteria and forms differ by jurisdiction. There is no single national mental health act.
Common trap: Assuming one national involuntary treatment standard applies across Australia.

Topic: Asking directly about suicide is safe and necessary
Hook: Asking does not plant the idea. Not asking leaves you guessing.
Australian practice: Australian crisis lines are Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636, and 13YARN 13 92 76, a national line staffed by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander crisis supporters.
Common trap: Avoiding the direct question, or giving a number that does not operate in Australia.

Topic: Alcohol withdrawal can kill. Opioid withdrawal usually does not.
Hook: The timeline tells you when to worry.
Australian practice: Withdrawal protocols follow state health department guidelines, and alcohol and drug information services are state-based rather than a single national line.
Common trap: Treating alcohol and opioid withdrawal as equally dangerous.
Resource: Australian Government, Alcohol and other drugs

Topic: Screening for family violence: ask them alone
Hook: You cannot screen safely with the partner in the room.
Australian practice: The national referral line is 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Mandatory reporting thresholds for child abuse differ by state. Culturally safe, trauma-informed responses are an explicit NMBA expectation.
Common trap: Asking screening questions with a family member still present.

Topic: Grief, and what cultural safety actually means
Hook: Cultural safety is judged by the person receiving care, not by you.
Australian practice: Cultural safety for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples is a codified NMBA obligation, not optional good practice. Kinship obligations and Sorry Business must be respected and accommodated, including flexibility about visitor numbers and ceremony.
Common trap: Applying a Western grief-stage model rigidly and missing kinship and community mourning practices.
Resource: NMBA: Joint statement on culturally safe care
